chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
title: Amy sings 'Ole Man River' on the ship home
summary: On the ship back, the singer Amy was pressed to sing Ole Man River; when she sang the original lyric's slur everyone fled, leaving Bill Coleman's foster daughter bewildered.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: and got all our ladyfriend, and there were some English people who followed us all around and there was a certain girl, tall beautiful girl, but she was just tall and beautiful. Her name was Amy. Well, Amy could sing, she had a deep voice, you know, a contralto voice, but it was a pleasant voice, but she could sing beautifully. Now, on the ship coming back, everybody's happy. I think Burns had a case full of — , of cocaine which was nothing to — about, just nothing, just — and everybody was happy.
We're all sitting on the deck and they said, Amy, go on and sing a song. Sing Ole' Man River, Amy. She said, I don't like that song, don't ask me to -- and they kept on bugging her.

Everybody around. Amy opened up with the first of Ole Man River which is written on the sheet. Niggers -- and when she said niggers everybody disappeared. Chiterson disappeared, everybody disappeared, and the only one that was left there, Bill Coleman had his little foster daughter, her name was -- I can't think of it, but she was there and everybody disappeared and she said, why is everybody running. Why is everybody running.

And the poor girl, she was crying and I said I told you fellows why do you do these things, and she got sick. She got sick, oh, all right, everybody's feeling good on the boat. Got a pocket full of money. We gets off the boat in Holland,
